newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Israel, Palestinians buoyant after Brussels talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians buoyant after Brussels talks.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian leaders on Tuesday held one of their most productive meetings for months, with both sides suggesting a breakthrough in the Middle East peace process was possible.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said they had made great strides in sweetening the bitterness of five months of acrimony over the deadlocked talks.
"I am highly satisfied with our discussions," Levy said after meeting Arafat for talks brokered by the European Union.
"Significant and positive steps have been taken," said Arafat.
The meeting, which lasted nearly an hour, was the highest-level contact between Israel and the Palestinians since the two men met in April on the fringes of an EU meeting in Malta.
It marked a significant triumph of diplomacy for the EU, which has long sought a greater role in Middle East peace negotiations.

"The whole system is no longer blocked," said Luxembourg's Foreign Minister Jacques Poos, who hosted the meeting on behalf of the EU presidency. "The atmosphere was excellant... We discussed ways in which the two parties might restart a dialogue."

Neither Arafat or Levy would elaborate during a later news conference on what had been agreed to accelerate a possible return to the negotiating table, but both stressed that the meeting was a breakthrough.
"I am sure we are now going to be able to establish the confidence neccessary to proceed," Levy said.
"We have to continue these meetings, especially as the peace process is facing serious problems," said Arafat.
Both Arafat and Levy appeared in good spirits, a far cry from the tense atmosphere that prevailed during their Malta meeting.
Arafat referred to Levy as "our cousin", adding: "I am firmly convinced that he sets great store by the peace process."
Levy said: "I am very satisfied with what I heard in the message from President Arafat."
Levy earlier gave a spirited defence of Israel's commitment to Middle East peace, telling European members of parliament that Israelis were "defending their lives."
"We see peace as a value and a goal, but it is a complicated issue," he told members of the European Parliament's foreign affairs committee.
"I know that some of you feel Israel is not helping the peace process, but this is not us being stubborn, this is us defending out lives," he said.
Levy was given a hostile reception, but he robustly defended Israeli policy, shouting at one heckler: "You have to be in Israel or with Israel to understand completely."
The Moroccan-born foreign minister, speaking a mixture of French and Hebrew, said: "I am not so naive as to believe I could have come here and changed opinions. All I can do is explain our position."
He reminded the committee of the threat Jews had faced in the past, particularly in Europe, adding: "We hate war ... we have been victims of a war that was designed to eradicate us completely.
"It is our right to expect from Europe...to allow the two sides to try to resolve the matter without interference."
The EU has long been a vociferous backer of Palestinian aspirations for a homeland and is the biggest bankroller of aid to the fledgling Palestinian Authority.
